notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Communication technology deals with transmission, reception and processing of information.
  • Information may be in the form of voice, text, image, video or data.
  • A basic communication system contains a transmitter, communication channel and receiver.
  • A message signal carries information.
  • The communication channel may be wired or wireless.
  • Noise is any unwanted disturbance that affects the transmitted signal.
  • Modern communication systems use electronics, electromagnetic waves, satellites, optical fibres and digital networks.
  • Communication technology is the foundation of radio, television, telephones, mobile networks and the internet.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Communication System → Transmitter → Channel → Receiver

2. Elements of a Communication System

Main elements are:

  • Information source.
  • Input transducer.
  • Transmitter.
  • Communication channel.
  • Receiver.
  • Output transducer.
  • Destination.
  • Noise may enter the communication channel.
3. Information Source
  • Information source generates the original message.
  • Human speech is an information source in a telephone system.
  • A computer can generate digital information.
  • A television camera generates image and video information.
4. Transducer
  • A transducer converts energy from one form to another.
  • An input transducer converts physical information into an electrical signal.
  • A microphone converts sound into an electrical signal.
  • A camera sensor converts light into electrical signals.
  • A loudspeaker is an output transducer.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Microphone → Sound to Electrical

Loudspeaker → Electrical to Sound

5. Transmitter
  • A transmitter prepares a signal for transmission.
  • It may amplify the signal.
  • It may encode information.
  • It may modulate a carrier wave.
  • It sends the processed signal through a communication channel.
6. Receiver
  • A receiver collects the transmitted signal.
  • It amplifies weak signals.
  • It selects the required signal from unwanted signals.
  • It demodulates or decodes information.
  • It sends recovered information to an output device.
7. Communication Channel
  • A communication channel carries information from transmitter to receiver.
  • Channels may be guided or unguided.
  • Copper cable is a guided medium.
  • Coaxial cable is a guided medium.
  • Optical fibre is a guided medium.
  • Free-space radio transmission is unguided.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Guided → Cable/Fibre

Unguided → Free-Space EM Waves

8. Noise
  • Noise is unwanted electrical or electromagnetic disturbance.
  • Noise can distort the original message.
  • Sources include thermal noise, atmospheric disturbances and electrical equipment.
  • Digital communication can use error-detection and correction methods to reduce the effects of noise.
9. Signal
  • A signal is a varying physical quantity that carries information.
  • Electrical voltage can be a signal.
  • Electric current can carry information.
  • Electromagnetic waves can carry information.
  • Optical pulses in fibre carry digital data.
10. Analog Signal
  • An analog signal varies continuously with time and amplitude.
  • Human speech converted by a microphone is initially analog.
  • Traditional AM and FM broadcasting use analog modulation.
  • Analog signals can take a continuous range of values.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Analog → Continuous

11. Digital Signal
  • A digital signal uses discrete levels.
  • Binary systems commonly use 0 and 1.
  • Digital signals are easier to store, process and regenerate.
  • Modern computers and mobile networks are primarily digital.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Digital → Discrete → 0 and 1

12. Analog vs Digital Communication
  • Analog communication transmits continuously varying signals.
  • Digital communication transmits coded discrete information.
  • Digital systems provide strong resistance to accumulated noise through regeneration.
  • Digital data can be compressed and encrypted easily.
  • Analog systems can be simpler in basic implementations.
13. Baseband Signal
  • Baseband signal is the original information signal before modulation onto a high-frequency carrier.
  • Voice and digital data can exist as baseband signals.
  • Baseband transmission is common over short wired links.
14. Carrier Wave
  • A carrier wave is a high-frequency electromagnetic signal used to transport information.
  • The information signal modifies one or more carrier properties.
  • Carrier frequency is usually much higher than the message frequency.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Carrier → High-Frequency Wave Carrying Information

15. Modulation
  • Modulation is the process of varying a property of a high-frequency carrier according to an information signal.
  • Modulation is necessary for efficient long-distance wireless communication.
  • It allows practical antenna sizes.
  • It enables multiple channels to operate at different carrier frequencies.
  • Common analog modulation methods are AM, FM and PM.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Modulation → Message + Carrier

16. Why Modulation Is Needed
  • Low-frequency signals are inefficient for direct radio transmission.
  • Practical antenna dimensions depend on wavelength.
  • Modulation shifts information to higher frequencies.
  • Different carrier frequencies prevent signals from different stations from overlapping.
  • Modulation increases communication range.
17. Amplitude Modulation
  • AM stands for Amplitude Modulation.
  • In AM, carrier amplitude varies according to message signal.
  • Carrier frequency remains essentially constant.
  • AM radio broadcasting traditionally uses amplitude modulation.
  • AM is more susceptible to amplitude noise than FM.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

AM → Amplitude Changes

18. Frequency Modulation
  • FM stands for Frequency Modulation.
  • In FM, carrier frequency varies according to the message signal.
  • Carrier amplitude remains approximately constant.
  • FM provides better resistance to amplitude noise.
  • FM radio is widely used for high-fidelity audio broadcasting.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

FM → Frequency Changes

19. Phase Modulation
  • PM stands for Phase Modulation.
  • In PM, carrier phase varies according to the message.
  • PM is closely related mathematically to frequency modulation.
  • Phase-modulation concepts are important in digital communication.
20. AM vs FM
  • AM varies amplitude.
  • FM varies frequency.
  • AM requires relatively smaller bandwidth in traditional broadcasting.
  • FM generally provides better noise immunity.
  • AM signals can travel long distances using suitable frequency bands.
  • FM broadcast signals are mainly line-of-sight.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

AM → Amplitude.

FM → Frequency.

21. Demodulation
  • Demodulation is the recovery of information from a modulated carrier.
  • A radio receiver demodulates the selected broadcast.
  • A demodulator is also called a detector in some systems.
  • Demodulation is the reverse functional process of modulation.
22. Bandwidth
  • Bandwidth is the range of frequencies occupied or supported by a communication channel or signal.
  • Higher bandwidth generally allows higher data rates.
  • Bandwidth is measured in hertz for frequency-domain systems.
  • Optical fibre provides very large bandwidth.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bandwidth ↑ → Potential Data Rate ↑

23. Electromagnetic Waves in Communication

Communication uses:

  • Radio waves.
  • Microwaves.
  • Infrared.
  • Visible and near-infrared light in optical systems.
  • Electromagnetic waves can travel through vacuum.
  • Their speed in vacuum is approximately 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
24. Radio Waves
  • Radio waves are electromagnetic waves used for broadcasting and communication.
  • They can be generated by accelerating electric charges in antennas.
  • Radio frequencies cover a broad range.
  • Different bands have different propagation characteristics.
25. Antenna
  • An antenna converts electrical signals into electromagnetic waves during transmission.
  • It converts incoming electromagnetic waves into electrical signals during reception.
  • Antenna size depends strongly on operating wavelength.
  • Higher-frequency systems can use smaller antennas.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Antenna → Electrical ↔ Electromagnetic Waves

26. Wavelength and Frequency
  • Electromagnetic-wave relation is c = fλ in vacuum.
  • Higher frequency means shorter wavelength.
  • Lower frequency means longer wavelength.
  • Antenna dimensions are commonly related to wavelength.
📌 Must-Memorise

c = fλ

27. Radio-Wave Propagation

Major propagation modes include:

  • Ground-wave propagation.
  • Sky-wave propagation.
  • Line-of-sight propagation.
28. Ground-Wave Propagation
  • Ground waves travel close to Earth's surface.
  • They can follow Earth's curvature to some extent.
  • They are most effective at lower radio frequencies.
  • Traditional AM broadcast in lower bands can use ground-wave propagation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ground Wave → Travels Along Earth's Surface

29. Sky-Wave Propagation
  • Sky waves return toward Earth after interaction with the ionosphere.
  • They enable communication beyond the horizon.
  • High-frequency shortwave radio can use sky-wave propagation.
  • The ionosphere contains ionised atmospheric layers.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sky Wave → Ionosphere

30. Ionosphere
  • The ionosphere is an ionised region of Earth's upper atmosphere.
  • Solar radiation ionises atmospheric particles.
  • It affects radio-wave propagation.
  • Some radio frequencies can be refracted back toward Earth.
  • Ionospheric conditions vary with time of day and solar activity.
31. Line-of-Sight Communication
  • Line-of-sight signals travel approximately straight between transmitting and receiving antennas.
  • VHF, UHF and microwave communication often use line-of-sight propagation.
  • Earth's curvature limits direct range.
  • Taller antennas increase line-of-sight range.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Microwave/VHF/UHF → Mainly Line-of-Sight

32. Microwave Communication
  • Microwaves are high-frequency electromagnetic waves.
  • They can carry large amounts of information.
  • Microwave communication is mainly line-of-sight.
  • Relay towers are used to extend terrestrial microwave links.
  • Satellite communication also uses microwave frequencies.
33. Microwave Relay Tower
  • Relay stations receive a microwave signal.
  • They amplify or regenerate it.
  • They retransmit it to the next station.
  • Towers are positioned within line of sight.
34. Satellite Communication
  • Communication satellites relay signals between widely separated locations.
  • Ground stations send signals to satellites.
  • The satellite receives, processes/amplifies and retransmits signals.
  • Satellite communication is used for television, telephony, internet and navigation services.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Satellite → Long-Distance Relay

35. Uplink
  • Uplink is transmission from an Earth station to a satellite.
  • The uplink frequency is generally different from the downlink frequency.
  • Frequency separation prevents interference between transmitted and received signals.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Earth → Satellite = Uplink

36. Downlink
  • Downlink is transmission from satellite to Earth station.
  • The satellite transmits received information toward target regions on Earth.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Satellite → Earth = Downlink

37. Transponder
  • A transponder is a key communication subsystem in a satellite.
  • It receives an uplink signal.
  • It filters and amplifies or regenerates the signal.
  • It changes frequency where required.
  • It retransmits the signal on the downlink.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Satellite Communication Unit → Transponder

38. Geostationary Satellite
  • A geostationary satellite appears fixed over one point on Earth's equator.
  • It orbits in the equatorial plane.
  • It moves in the same direction as Earth's rotation.
  • Its orbital period equals Earth's rotational period relative to the stars.
  • Its altitude is approximately 35,786 km above mean sea level.
  • It is useful for continuous communication coverage.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Geostationary Altitude → ~35,786 km

39. Conditions for Geostationary Orbit
  • Orbit must be circular.
  • Orbit must lie in Earth's equatorial plane.
  • Satellite must move west-to-east, same as Earth's rotation.
  • Orbital period must match Earth's sidereal rotation period.
  • It therefore appears stationary relative to a ground observer.
40. Geosynchronous vs Geostationary
  • A geosynchronous satellite has an orbital period equal to Earth's rotation period.
  • A geostationary satellite is a special geosynchronous satellite.
  • Geostationary orbit must additionally be circular and equatorial.
  • Not every geosynchronous satellite is geostationary.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

All geostationary satellites are geosynchronous.

Not all geosynchronous satellites are geostationary.

41. Polar Satellite
  • Polar satellites orbit approximately over Earth's poles.
  • Earth rotates beneath their orbit.
  • They can observe most or all of Earth's surface over time.
  • Polar satellites are useful for remote sensing, weather and Earth observation.
42. Communication Satellite vs Remote-Sensing Satellite
  • Communication satellites relay information signals.
  • Remote-sensing satellites collect information about Earth's surface and atmosphere.
  • Communication satellites often use geostationary orbit.
  • Remote-sensing satellites commonly use polar or sun-synchronous orbits.
43. Satellite Delay
  • Geostationary satellites are far from Earth.
  • Radio signals require a noticeable time to travel up and down.
  • This produces latency in satellite communication.
  • Low-Earth-orbit satellite systems have lower propagation delay.
44. Low Earth Orbit
  • LEO stands for Low Earth Orbit.
  • LEO satellites orbit much closer to Earth than geostationary satellites.
  • They have shorter orbital periods.
  • Communication constellations may use many LEO satellites for continuous coverage.
  • Lower altitude reduces signal delay.
45. Telephone
  • Telephone converts sound into electrical or digital signals.
  • Signals are transmitted through wired or wireless networks.
  • At the receiver, signals are converted back into sound.
  • Modern telephone networks are largely digital.
46. Alexander Graham Bell
  • Alexander Graham Bell is strongly associated with the development and patenting of the telephone.
  • Bell received a major U.S. telephone patent in 1876.
  • Telephone technology transformed long-distance communication.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Alexander Graham Bell → Telephone → 1876

47. Landline Telephone
  • Traditional landline systems use metallic wires or optical fibres.
  • Voice signals are converted into electrical or digital form.
  • Telephone exchanges route calls between users.
  • Modern fixed-line networks increasingly use digital and internet-based technologies.
48. Mobile Communication
  • Mobile communication uses radio links between mobile devices and base stations.
  • Service areas are divided into cells.
  • Each cell is served by one or more base stations.
  • Frequency reuse allows efficient use of radio spectrum.
  • Cellular networks support voice, messaging and data.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mobile Network → Cellular Concept

49. Cell in Cellular Network
  • A geographical service area is divided into cells.
  • Each cell is covered by a base station.
  • As a user moves, the network can transfer the connection between cells.
  • This process is called handover or handoff.
50. Base Transceiver Station
  • BTS stands for Base Transceiver Station.
  • It contains radio equipment communicating with mobile devices.
  • Antennas transmit and receive cellular signals.
  • Modern network terminology differs by generation, but the base-station concept remains fundamental.
51. Handover
  • Handover transfers an active mobile connection from one base station or cell to another.
  • It allows communication to continue while the user moves.
  • Network systems choose a suitable neighbouring cell based on signal and network conditions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Moving Mobile User → Handover

52. SIM
  • SIM stands for Subscriber Identity Module.
  • It stores subscriber identity and authentication information.
  • SIM enables a device to identify itself to a mobile network.
  • eSIM provides similar functions electronically without a removable physical card.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

SIM → Subscriber Identity Module

53. IMEI
  • IMEI stands for International Mobile Equipment Identity.
  • It identifies a mobile device, not the subscriber account.
  • SIM identifies the subscriber relationship.
  • IMEI identifies the equipment.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

SIM → Subscriber.

IMEI → Device.

54. Cellular Generations

Common broad progression:

  • 1G → Analog mobile voice.
  • 2G → Digital voice and basic data.
  • 3G → Higher-speed mobile data.
  • 4G → Broadband all-IP mobile communication.
  • 5G → Higher capacity, lower latency and support for massive device connectivity.
55. 1G
  • First-generation cellular systems were primarily analog.
  • They supported voice communication.
  • Data capability was very limited.
56. 2G
  • 2G introduced digital cellular communication.
  • GSM became a major 2G standard.
  • SMS became widely used.
  • Digital systems improved capacity and security compared with 1G.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

2G → Digital Voice + SMS

57. GSM
  • GSM stands for Global System for Mobile Communications.
  • It became one of the world's dominant second-generation mobile standards.
  • GSM uses SIM-based subscriber identity.
  • It supports voice, SMS and data extensions.
58. SMS
  • SMS stands for Short Message Service.
  • It allows short text messages to be exchanged over mobile networks.
  • SMS became widely popular with 2G cellular systems.
59. 3G
  • 3G increased mobile-data capability.
  • It enabled more practical mobile internet access, video calling and multimedia services.
  • 3G represented a transition toward broadband mobile communication.
60. 4G
  • 4G provides high-speed mobile broadband.
  • LTE is a major 4G technology family.
  • 4G networks use packet-switched, all-IP architecture for data services.
  • Voice may be provided using VoLTE.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

4G → LTE → Broadband IP Network

61. LTE
  • LTE stands for Long-Term Evolution.
  • LTE is associated with fourth-generation mobile broadband.
  • It provides high data rates and low latency compared with earlier generations.
62. VoLTE
  • VoLTE stands for Voice over LTE.
  • It carries voice calls as IP-based traffic over LTE networks.
  • It can provide faster call setup and improved voice quality.
63. 5G
  • 5G is the fifth generation of mobile communication technology.
  • It supports higher data rates.
  • It can provide lower latency.
  • It supports very large numbers of connected devices.
  • It uses a range of radio-frequency bands.
  • Technologies include massive MIMO and beamforming.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

5G → High Capacity + Low Latency + Massive Connectivity

64. MIMO
  • MIMO stands for Multiple Input Multiple Output.
  • It uses multiple transmitting and receiving antennas.
  • MIMO can increase data capacity and reliability.
  • It is used in Wi-Fi, 4G and 5G systems.
65. Beamforming
  • Beamforming directs radio energy toward selected users or directions.
  • It uses multiple antenna elements and controlled signal phases.
  • Beamforming improves signal quality and spectrum efficiency.
  • It is important in modern cellular and Wi-Fi systems.
66. Wi-Fi
  • Wi-Fi provides wireless local-area networking.
  • It uses radio waves.
  • It is based on IEEE 802.11 standards.
  • Wi-Fi connects devices to local networks and internet gateways.
  • Wi-Fi is not the same as cellular mobile data.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Wi-Fi → IEEE 802.11

67. WLAN
  • WLAN stands for Wireless Local Area Network.
  • Wi-Fi is the most common WLAN technology.
  • WLAN provides local wireless connectivity within homes, offices and public spaces.
68. Bluetooth
  • Bluetooth is a short-range wireless communication technology.
  • It operates in the 2.4 GHz industrial, scientific and medical band.
  • It is used for headphones, keyboards, wearables and device-to-device communication.
  • Bluetooth Low Energy is designed for low-power applications.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bluetooth → Short-Range Wireless → 2.4 GHz Band

69. NFC
  • NFC stands for Near Field Communication.
  • It operates over very short distances.
  • It is used in contactless payments, access cards and device pairing.
  • NFC uses electromagnetic coupling.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

NFC → Very Short Range

70. RFID
  • RFID stands for Radio-Frequency Identification.
  • RFID systems use radio waves to identify tagged objects.
  • Tags may be passive or active.
  • RFID is used in inventory control, tolling and access systems.
71. Infrared Communication
  • Infrared light can carry information.
  • Television remote controls commonly use infrared.
  • Infrared links generally require short range and approximate line of sight.
  • Infrared does not penetrate opaque walls effectively.
72. Optical-Fibre Communication
  • Optical fibre transmits information using pulses of light.
  • The fibre core has higher refractive index than cladding.
  • Light is guided mainly by total internal reflection.
  • Optical fibres provide high bandwidth.
  • They have low transmission loss over long distances.
  • They are immune to ordinary electromagnetic interference.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Optical Fibre → Total Internal Reflection

73. Fibre Structure

Main parts include:

  • Core.
  • Cladding.
  • Protective coating.
  • Core carries light.
  • Cladding has lower refractive index.
  • Protective layers provide mechanical strength.
74. Fibre-Optic Advantages
  • Very high bandwidth.
  • Low attenuation.
  • Small size and low weight.
  • Electrical isolation.
  • Resistance to electromagnetic interference.
  • High security against simple electromagnetic interception.
75. Fibre-Optic Disadvantages
  • Fibre can be fragile if improperly handled.
  • Splicing and connector installation require precision.
  • Optical-electrical conversion equipment is required.
  • Tight bending can increase signal loss.
76. Laser Diode in Fibre Communication
  • Laser diodes are common high-speed optical sources.
  • Semiconductor lasers provide narrow and intense beams.
  • LEDs can also be used for shorter or lower-speed optical links.
  • Laser sources are preferred for many long-distance high-capacity systems.
77. Photodetector
  • A photodetector converts incoming optical signals into electrical signals.
  • Photodiodes are widely used in fibre receivers.
  • Light creates charge carriers in the detector.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Fibre Receiver → Photodiode

78. Attenuation
  • Attenuation is reduction in signal strength during transmission.
  • It occurs in electrical cables, radio channels and optical fibres.
  • Repeaters or amplifiers compensate for attenuation.
  • Fibre has very low attenuation at suitable wavelengths.
79. Repeater
  • A repeater receives a weakened signal.
  • It amplifies or regenerates it.
  • It retransmits the restored signal.
  • Repeaters extend communication range.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Repeater → Extends Signal Range

80. Amplifier vs Repeater
  • An amplifier increases signal strength along with any noise present.
  • A digital repeater can regenerate clean signal levels.
  • Repeaters are especially useful in digital networks.
81. Multiplexing
  • Multiplexing allows multiple signals to share one communication channel.
  • It increases channel efficiency.
  • Different users may be separated by frequency, time, wavelength or code.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Multiplexing → Many Signals on One Channel

82. Frequency-Division Multiplexing
  • FDM stands for Frequency-Division Multiplexing.
  • Different signals occupy different frequency bands simultaneously.
  • Traditional radio broadcasting is an intuitive example of frequency separation.
83. Time-Division Multiplexing
  • TDM stands for Time-Division Multiplexing.
  • Different users share a channel at different time slots.
  • It is widely used in digital communication.
84. Wavelength-Division Multiplexing
  • WDM stands for Wavelength-Division Multiplexing.
  • It sends multiple optical wavelengths through the same fibre.
  • Each wavelength carries separate data.
  • WDM greatly increases fibre capacity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

WDM → Multiple Colours/Wavelengths in One Fibre

85. Coding
  • Coding represents information using symbols or binary patterns.
  • Digital communication uses coding for efficient transmission.
  • Coding can provide error detection and correction.
  • Compression reduces the number of bits required.
86. Encryption
  • Encryption converts readable information into coded form.
  • It protects information from unauthorised access.
  • A key is used to encrypt and decrypt data in cryptographic systems.
  • Secure internet communication relies heavily on encryption.
87. Internet
  • The internet is a global network of interconnected computer networks.
  • It uses the Internet Protocol suite.
  • Data is transmitted in packets.
  • Routers direct packets between networks.
  • The internet supports web, email, streaming, messaging and many other services.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Internet → Network of Networks

88. Packet Switching
  • Packet switching divides data into smaller packets.
  • Packets can travel through different network routes.
  • The destination reassembles the data.
  • Packet switching efficiently shares network resources.
  • The internet is fundamentally packet-switched.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Internet → Packet Switching

89. IP
  • IP stands for Internet Protocol.
  • It provides addressing and routing of packets across networks.
  • IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses.
  • IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses.
  • IPv6 provides a vastly larger address space.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

IPv4 → 32 bit

IPv6 → 128 bit

90. TCP
  • TCP stands for Transmission Control Protocol.
  • It provides reliable ordered delivery of data between applications.
  • TCP detects lost data and retransmits it.
  • TCP works together with IP.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

TCP → Reliable Delivery

91. UDP
  • UDP stands for User Datagram Protocol.
  • It provides fast connectionless data transmission.
  • It does not guarantee delivery or ordering.
  • It is used where low latency is more important than perfect delivery.
92. Router
  • A router connects different computer networks.
  • It examines packet addresses.
  • It selects paths for forwarding packets.
  • Home routers commonly connect local devices to the internet.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Router → Connects Networks

93. Modem
  • Modem stands for Modulator-Demodulator.
  • It converts information into a form suitable for a communication link and recovers it at the receiver.
  • Traditional telephone modems converted digital computer data to analog signals and back.
  • Modern broadband devices may still be called modems even when using different physical technologies.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

MODEM → Modulator + Demodulator

94. Switch in Computer Networks
  • A network switch connects devices within a local network.
  • It forwards data based mainly on hardware addresses at the data-link layer.
  • It is different from an electrical switch and from a router.
95. LAN
  • LAN stands for Local Area Network.
  • It covers a limited area such as a building, school or office.
  • Ethernet and Wi-Fi are common LAN technologies.
96. WAN
  • WAN stands for Wide Area Network.
  • It covers large geographical areas.
  • The internet is the largest example of interconnected wide-area networking.
97. Ethernet
  • Ethernet is a widely used wired LAN technology.
  • It is standardised under IEEE 802.3.
  • Ethernet commonly uses twisted-pair or optical-fibre links.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ethernet → IEEE 802.3

98. World Wide Web
  • The World Wide Web is a service operating over the internet.
  • It uses interconnected web pages and resources.
  • Tim Berners-Lee developed the World Wide Web at CERN around 1989–1990.
  • The web is not the same as the internet.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tim Berners-Lee → World Wide Web

99. Internet vs World Wide Web
  • Internet → Global network infrastructure.
  • World Wide Web → Information service using web pages over the internet.
  • Email can use the internet without using the web directly.
  • Therefore, web and internet are not identical.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Internet ≠ World Wide Web

100. URL
  • URL stands for Uniform Resource Locator.
  • It identifies the location of a resource on a network.
  • Web browsers use URLs to access webpages and other resources.
101. HTTP
  • HTTP stands for Hypertext Transfer Protocol.
  • It is used for transferring web resources.
  • HTTPS is HTTP protected using cryptographic security through TLS.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

HTTPS → Secure Web Communication

102. Email
  • Email means electronic mail.
  • It sends digital messages over computer networks.
  • SMTP is commonly used for sending email.
  • IMAP and POP are used for retrieving email.
103. Cloud Computing
  • Cloud computing provides computing resources over networks.
  • Services may include storage, software and processing.
  • Data is stored and processed in remote data centres.
  • Users access services through internet connections.
104. Internet of Things
  • IoT stands for Internet of Things.
  • IoT connects physical devices to communication networks.
  • Devices may contain sensors, processors and wireless modules.
  • Applications include smart homes, agriculture, healthcare and industry.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

IoT → Connected Physical Devices

105. Satellite Navigation
  • Satellite-navigation systems determine location using signals from satellites.
  • A receiver measures signal travel times from multiple satellites.
  • Position is calculated using trilateration.
  • Accurate timing is essential.
  • Atomic clocks are used aboard navigation satellites.
106. GPS
  • GPS stands for Global Positioning System.
  • It was developed by the United States.
  • It uses a constellation of navigation satellites.
  • GPS provides position, navigation and timing information globally.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

GPS → United States

107. NavIC
  • NavIC stands for Navigation with Indian Constellation.
  • It is India's regional satellite-navigation system.
  • It was developed by ISRO.
  • It was formerly known as IRNSS.
  • It provides positioning services over India and a surrounding regional area.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

NavIC → India → ISRO

108. IRNSS
  • IRNSS stands for Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System.
  • The system's operational service is known as NavIC.
  • It is designed primarily for regional navigation.
109. GPS vs NavIC
  • GPS is a global navigation system developed by the United States.
  • NavIC is an Indian regional navigation system.
  • Both provide position and timing services using satellite signals.
  • NavIC was developed by ISRO.
110. Trilateration
  • Satellite positioning uses distances from several satellites.
  • Three-dimensional position and receiver clock correction require signals from multiple satellites.
  • This method is called trilateration rather than triangulation in the basic distance-based sense.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

GPS positioning → Mainly trilateration, not ordinary angle triangulation.

111. RADAR
  • RADAR stands for Radio Detection and Ranging.
  • It transmits radio or microwave signals.
  • Reflected waves are detected.
  • Distance can be calculated from travel time.
  • Radar is used in aviation, weather, defence and speed measurement.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

RADAR → Radio Detection and Ranging

112. Radar Distance Formula
  • Electromagnetic pulse travels to target and back.
  • Distance d = ct/2.
  • c is speed of electromagnetic waves.
  • t is round-trip travel time.
113. Doppler Radar
  • Doppler radar uses frequency shift to measure relative velocity.
  • It is used to measure vehicle speed.
  • Weather radar uses Doppler shift to estimate motion of precipitation.
  • It applies the Doppler effect.
114. Weather Radar
  • Weather radar transmits microwave pulses.
  • Rain, hail and other particles reflect part of the signal.
  • Returned signals reveal precipitation intensity and motion.
  • Doppler weather radar measures radial velocity.
115. LIDAR
  • LIDAR stands for Light Detection and Ranging.
  • It uses laser pulses rather than radio waves.
  • It measures distance using travel time.
  • It is used in mapping, atmospheric science and autonomous systems.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

RADAR → Radio

LIDAR → Laser Light

116. SONAR
  • SONAR stands for Sound Navigation and Ranging.
  • It uses sound waves.
  • It is mainly used underwater.
  • SONAR differs from radar because it uses mechanical sound waves rather than electromagnetic waves.
📌 Must-Memorise

RADAR → Radio

LIDAR → Light

SONAR → Sound

117. Television Communication
  • Television transmits moving images and sound.
  • Traditional analog television modulated radio-frequency carriers.
  • Modern digital television compresses and transmits digital audio and video data.
  • Television may be terrestrial, cable, satellite or internet-based.
118. Television Camera
  • A television camera converts light from a scene into electrical or digital signals.
  • Modern cameras use semiconductor image sensors such as CCD or CMOS sensors.
119. CCD
  • CCD stands for Charge-Coupled Device.
  • It is a semiconductor image sensor.
  • It converts incoming light into electrical charge patterns.
  • CCDs have been widely used in cameras and astronomy.
120. CMOS Image Sensor
  • CMOS image sensors are semiconductor image detectors.
  • CMOS stands for Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor.
  • They are widely used in smartphones and digital cameras.
  • They integrate sensing and processing circuitry efficiently.
121. Digital Television
  • Digital TV transmits encoded digital video and audio.
  • Digital compression allows efficient use of bandwidth.
  • Error-correction techniques improve reception quality.
  • Multiple channels can be carried within spectrum previously occupied by fewer analog channels.
122. Radio Broadcasting
  • Radio broadcasting transmits audio information using electromagnetic waves.
  • AM and FM are common broadcasting methods.
  • A receiver selects a station using tuning circuits.
  • Demodulation recovers audio information.
123. AM Broadcast
  • AM broadcasting uses amplitude modulation.
  • AM signals can use ground-wave and sky-wave propagation depending on frequency.
  • It can cover long distances.
  • It is more susceptible to electrical noise than FM.
124. FM Broadcast
  • FM broadcasting uses frequency modulation.
  • It offers better noise immunity.
  • FM broadcasts usually operate in VHF bands.
  • Coverage is mainly line-of-sight.
  • FM generally provides better audio quality.
125. Satellite Television
  • Satellite television sends broadcast signals to communication satellites.
  • Satellites retransmit them to receiving dishes.
  • Receiving dish antennas focus microwave signals onto a receiver.
  • Geostationary satellites are widely used.
126. Dish Antenna
  • A parabolic dish reflects incoming parallel microwave signals toward a focal point.
  • A feed antenna or receiver is positioned near the focus.
  • Large dish diameter improves signal collection and directional gain.
127. Cable Television
  • Cable television distributes signals through coaxial cable and/or optical fibre.
  • It avoids dependence on direct terrestrial broadcast reception.
  • Modern cable systems also provide broadband internet.
128. Coaxial Cable
  • Coaxial cable has a central conductor surrounded by insulation and conducting shield.
  • The shield reduces electromagnetic interference.
  • Coaxial cable carries higher-frequency signals better than simple unshielded wires.
  • It has been widely used for television and broadband networks.
129. Twisted-Pair Cable
  • Twisted-pair cable contains pairs of insulated conductors twisted together.
  • Twisting reduces electromagnetic interference and crosstalk.
  • Telephone and Ethernet networks commonly use twisted-pair cables.
130. Optical Fibre vs Copper Cable
  • Fibre uses light.
  • Copper uses electrical signals.
  • Fibre offers greater bandwidth.
  • Fibre has lower attenuation over long distances.
  • Fibre is immune to electromagnetic interference.
  • Copper is often simpler for short electrical connections.
131. Communication Data Rate
  • Data rate measures amount of digital information transmitted per unit time.
  • Basic unit is bit per second.
  • Common multiples are kbps, Mbps and Gbps.
  • Higher bandwidth can support higher data rates.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Data Rate → bit/s

132. Bit Rate
  • Bit rate is number of bits transmitted per second.
  • 1 kbps is conventionally used as approximately 1000 bits/s in communication contexts.
  • 1 Mbps is approximately 10⁶ bits/s.
  • 1 Gbps is approximately 10⁹ bits/s.
133. Latency
  • Latency is delay between sending information and receiving or responding to it.
  • Propagation time contributes to latency.
  • Processing and network congestion also contribute.
  • Lower latency is important for interactive applications.
134. Signal-to-Noise Ratio
  • SNR stands for Signal-to-Noise Ratio.
  • It compares desired signal strength with noise strength.
  • Higher SNR generally means better signal quality.
  • SNR is often expressed in decibels.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

High SNR → Better Signal Quality

135. Shannon's Communication Link
  • Claude Shannon developed mathematical information theory.
  • He established fundamental limits on reliable communication over noisy channels.
  • The Shannon capacity theorem relates bandwidth, signal-to-noise ratio and maximum theoretical data rate.
  • Shannon is often called the father of information theory.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Claude Shannon → Information Theory

136. Claude Shannon
  • Claude Shannon published his landmark work on mathematical theory of communication in 1948.
  • He formalised the concept of information measured in bits.
  • His work forms the foundation of digital communication and coding theory.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Shannon → 1948 → Information Theory

137. Guglielmo Marconi
  • Guglielmo Marconi pioneered practical wireless telegraphy.
  • He demonstrated long-distance radio communication.
  • He shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics with Karl Ferdinand Braun.
  • Marconi is strongly associated with early radio communication.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Marconi → Wireless Telegraphy / Radio

138. Heinrich Hertz
  • Heinrich Hertz experimentally demonstrated electromagnetic waves in the late 1880s.
  • His work confirmed Maxwell's predictions.
  • The SI unit of frequency, hertz, is named after him.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hertz → Experimental EM Waves

139. James Clerk Maxwell
  • James Clerk Maxwell unified electricity and magnetism.
  • His equations predicted electromagnetic waves.
  • He showed that light is electromagnetic radiation.
  • Maxwell's work provided the theoretical foundation for wireless communication.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Maxwell → Predicted EM Waves

140. Jagadish Chandra Bose
  • Jagadish Chandra Bose conducted pioneering experiments with millimetre-wave and microwave radiation.
  • He demonstrated wireless signalling at short distances in the 1890s.
  • He developed important microwave components and detectors.
  • He is an important Indian pioneer in radio and microwave science.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

J. C. Bose → Early Microwave/Wireless Experiments

141. Sir C. V. Raman — Communication Link
  • Raman's discovery of inelastic light scattering underlies Raman spectroscopy.
  • Modern optical-fibre systems may use Raman amplification.
  • His work is important in optics, though he was not a communication-system inventor.
142. Arthur C. Clarke
  • Arthur C. Clarke popularised the concept of using geostationary satellites for global communication.
  • In 1945, he described communication satellites in geostationary orbit.
  • The geostationary orbit is sometimes informally called the Clarke orbit.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Arthur C. Clarke → Geostationary Communication Satellites → 1945

143. Communication Satellites in India
  • India uses communication satellites for telecommunication, broadcasting, meteorology and data services.
  • INSAT and GSAT series have played major roles.
  • ISRO develops and operates many Indian communication satellites.
  • Satellite communication supports television, weather services and emergency communications.
144. INSAT
  • INSAT stands for Indian National Satellite System.
  • It is a multipurpose satellite system.
  • INSAT services include telecommunications, television broadcasting, meteorology and search-and-rescue support.
  • The INSAT system began in the early 1980s.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

INSAT → Multipurpose Indian Satellite System

145. APPLE Satellite
  • APPLE stood for Ariane Passenger Payload Experiment.
  • It was India's first experimental communication satellite.
  • It was launched in 1981.
  • APPLE was an important step in India's communication-satellite development.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

APPLE → Experimental Communication Satellite → 1981

146. GSAT
  • GSAT refers to a family of Indian communication satellites.
  • GSAT satellites support telecommunications, broadcasting and data connectivity.
  • Different GSAT missions carry different communication payloads.
147. EDUSAT
  • EDUSAT was India's first satellite dedicated primarily to educational services.
  • It was launched in 2004.
  • It was also designated GSAT-3.
  • It supported distance education and classroom connectivity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

EDUSAT → GSAT-3 → Education → 2004

148. Telemedicine
  • Telemedicine uses communication networks to provide medical consultation and health services over distance.
  • Satellite and internet links can connect remote hospitals with specialists.
  • It is especially useful in geographically isolated areas.
149. Tele-education
  • Tele-education delivers educational content through communication technologies.
  • Satellite television, video conferencing and internet platforms can be used.
  • EDUSAT supported satellite-based educational communication in India.
150. Remote Sensing Communication Link
  • Remote-sensing satellites gather Earth-observation data.
  • Satellite data are transmitted to ground stations.
  • Communication systems are required to downlink images and measurements.
  • Remote sensing and communication satellites perform different primary functions.
151. Disaster Communication
  • Satellite communication can remain useful when terrestrial infrastructure is damaged.
  • Emergency networks provide communication during floods, cyclones and earthquakes.
  • Radio systems are important for disaster-response teams.
  • Communication redundancy improves resilience.
152. Ham Radio
  • Amateur radio is commonly called ham radio.
  • Licensed operators communicate using allocated radio-frequency bands.
  • Amateur radio can support emergency communication when other systems fail.
  • It is also used for technical experimentation.
153. Broadcasting vs Point-to-Point Communication
  • Broadcasting sends information from one transmitter to many receivers.
  • Radio and television broadcasting are examples.
  • Point-to-point communication connects a specific sender and receiver.
  • Telephone communication is primarily point-to-point.
154. Simplex Communication
  • Simplex communication allows transmission in only one direction.
  • Traditional broadcast radio is an example.
  • Keyboard-to-computer input can be treated as simplex in simplified examples.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Simplex → One Direction Only

155. Half-Duplex Communication
  • Half-duplex communication allows transmission in both directions, but not simultaneously.
  • Walkie-talkies are a classic example.
  • Users take turns transmitting.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Half-Duplex → Both Directions, One at a Time

156. Full-Duplex Communication
  • Full-duplex communication allows simultaneous communication in both directions.
  • Telephone conversation is a common example.
  • Modern network links can support full-duplex operation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Full-Duplex → Both Directions Simultaneously

157. Communication Modes — Must Remember
  • Simplex → One-way only.
  • Half-duplex → Two-way, one at a time.
  • Full-duplex → Two-way simultaneously.
158. Error Detection
  • Digital communication uses error-detection methods.
  • Parity bits can detect some errors.
  • Checksums and cyclic redundancy checks are widely used.
  • Error-detection allows corrupted data to be identified.
159. Error Correction
  • Error-correcting codes add redundant information.
  • The receiver can detect and sometimes correct errors without retransmission.
  • Such techniques are important in satellite and deep-space communication.
160. Compression
  • Compression reduces the amount of data required to represent information.
  • Lossless compression reproduces original data exactly.
  • Lossy compression removes some information to achieve greater size reduction.
  • Audio, image and video communication often uses compression.
161. Deep-Space Communication
  • Deep-space communication uses highly sensitive antennas and powerful transmitters.
  • Radio waves are commonly used.
  • Signal strength becomes extremely weak over interplanetary distances.
  • Large dish antennas and error-correction techniques are required.
  • Communication delay increases with distance.
162. Deep Space Network
  • Deep-space networks use large ground antennas placed at widely separated locations around Earth.
  • This arrangement allows continuous communication with distant spacecraft as Earth rotates.
  • Precise radio tracking also provides spacecraft position and velocity information.
163. Communication with Spacecraft
  • Commands are sent by uplink.
  • Scientific data return through downlink.
  • Radio-frequency systems are most common.
  • Some modern missions are testing laser communication for higher data rates.
164. Electromagnetic Spectrum — Communication Uses
  • Radio waves → Broadcasting and mobile communication.
  • Microwaves → Satellite, radar and cellular links.
  • Infrared → Remote controls and short-range optical links.
  • Visible/near-infrared → Fibre optics and laser communication.
165. Important Communication Formulae
  • Electromagnetic-wave relation → c = fλ.
  • Radar/LIDAR range → d = ct/2.
  • Satellite/communication delay → Time = Distance/Speed.
  • Data rate → Bits/Time.
  • Frequency → f = 1/T.
  • Signal-to-noise ratio → Desired signal power / Noise power.
166. Important Units
  • Frequency → Hertz.
  • Wavelength → Metre.
  • Data rate → bit/s.
  • Bandwidth → Hertz.
  • Signal level → Often decibel.
  • Electromagnetic-wave speed → m/s.
  • Satellite altitude → kilometre.

  • AM → Amplitude Modulation.
  • FM → Frequency Modulation.
  • GSM → Global System for Mobile Communications.
  • LTE → Long-Term Evolution.
  • SIM → Subscriber Identity Module.
  • IMEI → International Mobile Equipment Identity.

  • LIDAR → Light Detection and Ranging.
  • SONAR → Sound Navigation and Ranging.
  • MODEM → Modulator-Demodulator.
  • IoT → Internet of Things.
  • INSAT → Indian National Satellite System.
168. Important Scientist–Fact Pairs
  • James Clerk Maxwell → Predicted electromagnetic waves.
  • Heinrich Hertz → Demonstrated electromagnetic waves.
  • Guglielmo Marconi → Practical wireless telegraphy.
  • Alexander Graham Bell → Telephone.
  • Jagadish Chandra Bose → Microwave/wireless experiments.
  • Claude Shannon → Information theory.
  • Tim Berners-Lee → World Wide Web.
  • Arthur C. Clarke → Geostationary communication-satellite concept.
169. Important Dates
  • Bell telephone patent → 1876.
  • Hertz electromagnetic-wave experiments → Late 1880s.
  • Marconi wireless work → 1890s.
  • Clarke geostationary communication proposal → 1945.
  • Shannon information-theory paper → 1948.
  • APPLE satellite → 1981.
  • World Wide Web development → 1989–1990.
  • EDUSAT launch → 2004.
170. TNPSC Traps
  • Communication system requires transmitter, channel and receiver.
  • Analog signals vary continuously.
  • Digital signals use discrete levels.
  • Modulation is different from demodulation.
  • AM changes carrier amplitude.
  • FM changes carrier frequency.
  • FM generally has better noise immunity than AM.
  • Radio waves are electromagnetic and can travel through vacuum.
  • Sound waves require a medium.
  • Ground waves follow Earth's surface.
  • Sky waves involve the ionosphere.
  • Microwave links are mainly line-of-sight.
  • Uplink → Earth to satellite.
  • Downlink → Satellite to Earth.
  • Transponder is a satellite relay unit.
  • Geostationary orbit lies above equator.
  • Geostationary satellite appears stationary.
  • Not every geosynchronous satellite is geostationary.
  • Polar satellites are useful for Earth observation.
  • Mobile networks divide coverage into cells.
  • SIM identifies subscriber; IMEI identifies equipment.
  • 2G introduced digital mobile systems.
  • 4G is strongly associated with LTE.
  • Wi-Fi is not cellular mobile data.
  • Bluetooth is short-range.
  • Optical fibre uses total internal reflection.
  • Fibre core has higher refractive index than cladding.
  • Repeater extends transmission range.
  • WDM sends multiple optical wavelengths through one fibre.
  • Internet and World Wide Web are not the same.
  • IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses.
  • IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses.
  • Router connects networks.
  • Modem means modulator-demodulator.
  • GPS is U.S.-developed.
  • NavIC is Indian and developed by ISRO.
  • Satellite navigation mainly uses trilateration.
  • RADAR uses radio/microwaves.
  • LIDAR uses laser light.
  • SONAR uses sound.
  • Full-duplex allows simultaneous two-way communication.
  • APPLE was India's experimental communication satellite.
  • EDUSAT was dedicated primarily to education.
